originalCompanies.name: Apple Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Designs premium smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables, and a growing suite of subscription services tied together by its own operating systems and chips.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Roughly half of revenue comes from iPhone sales; a fast-growing, high-margin Services segment (App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, payments) supplies most of the rest.
originalCompanies.fact: Started in a garage by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne; the 2007 launch of a touchscreen phone reshaped the industry.
originalCompanies.history: Shares rallied in 2020–21 on record device demand and a 4-for-1 split, slid with tech during the 2022 rate-hike selloff, then reached new highs as buybacks and Services growth continued.

originalCompanies.name: Microsoft Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: Sells cloud computing infrastructure, productivity software, operating systems, developer tools, and gaming, with deep enterprise relationships worldwide.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Cloud services (Azure) and commercial software subscriptions such as Office 365 drive the bulk of revenue, alongside Windows licensing, LinkedIn, and gaming.
originalCompanies.fact: Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen; an early operating system licensed to IBM became its foundation.
originalCompanies.history: Cloud growth carried the stock through 2021, a 2022 drawdown followed rising rates, and a multi-billion-dollar AI partnership helped spark a strong 2023–24 rally.

originalCompanies.name: NVIDIA Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: Designs graphics processors and accelerated computing platforms that power gaming PCs and, increasingly, the data centers used to train and run artificial intelligence models.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Data-center chips and networking now generate the vast majority of revenue, with gaming GPUs, professional visualization, and automotive making up the rest.
originalCompanies.fact: Co-founded by Jensen Huang over a meal at a Denny’s; its parallel-computing software platform became an industry standard for AI research.
originalCompanies.history: A crypto and gaming boom lifted shares in 2021, a sharp 2022 decline followed, then surging demand for AI data-center chips drove one of the largest rallies in market history in 2023–24.

originalCompanies.name: Amazon.com, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Runs one of the world’s largest online marketplaces and logistics networks while also operating a leading cloud computing platform and a digital advertising business.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Online and third-party seller services bring in most revenue, but the cloud computing division and advertising generate an outsized share of operating profit.
originalCompanies.fact: Began as an online bookstore run out of its founder Jeff Bezos’s garage.
originalCompanies.history: Pandemic shopping lifted shares in 2020, an overbuilt fulfillment network and rising rates hurt in 2022, and cost cuts plus cloud and ad growth fueled a 2023–24 recovery.

originalCompanies.name: Alphabet Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Operates the world’s most-used search engine, a dominant video platform, a mobile operating system, and a fast-growing cloud business, plus long-term bets like self-driving cars.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Advertising across search and video generates most revenue; cloud services, subscriptions, and hardware make up the remainder.
originalCompanies.fact: Started as a Stanford research project by Larry Page and Sergey Brin; its name is a play on a very large number.
originalCompanies.history: Digital-ad strength pushed shares higher in 2021, an ad slowdown weighed in 2022, and investor worries about AI competition alternated with strong cloud results through 2024–25.

originalCompanies.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Owns several of the largest social networking and messaging apps on the planet and invests heavily in virtual reality hardware and artificial intelligence.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Nearly all revenue comes from targeted advertising across its family of social apps; its virtual-reality division loses billions per year.
originalCompanies.fact: Launched from a Harvard dorm room by Mark Zuckerberg; renamed itself in 2021 to signal a bet on the "metaverse."
originalCompanies.history: Shares fell more than 70% from their 2021 peak amid ad-tracking changes and heavy VR spending, then roughly quadrupled after a 2023 "year of efficiency."

originalCompanies.name: Tesla, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Designs and builds electric vehicles, battery storage systems, and solar products, and develops driver-assistance software.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Most revenue comes from selling electric cars; energy storage, regulatory credits, and services contribute the rest.
originalCompanies.fact: Led for years by Elon Musk; named after a famous inventor of alternating-current electrical systems.
originalCompanies.history: Shares surged roughly tenfold in 2020 and joined the S&P 500, fell sharply in 2022, and have swung widely on delivery numbers and autonomy hopes since.

originalCompanies.name: Netflix, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Operates a global subscription streaming service with original films and series, available in more than 190 countries.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Monthly membership fees generate nearly all revenue, supplemented by a newer ad-supported tier.
originalCompanies.fact: Began by mailing DVDs in red envelopes before pivoting to streaming.
originalCompanies.history: Shares crashed about 75% in 2022 after reporting its first subscriber loss in a decade, then soared after a password-sharing crackdown and launch of an ad tier.

originalCompanies.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
originalCompanies.blurb: The largest bank in the United States by assets, spanning consumer banking, credit cards, investment banking, trading, and asset management.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Earns net interest income on loans and deposits plus fees from investment banking, trading, payments, and wealth management.
originalCompanies.fact: Traces its roots to a water company co-founded by Aaron Burr in 1799; led by Jamie Dimon since 2005.
originalCompanies.history: Higher interest rates boosted lending profits in 2022–23, and the bank acquired First Republic during the 2023 regional bank crisis.

originalCompanies.name: Visa Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Runs a global electronic payments network that connects consumers, merchants, and banks, without lending money itself.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Charges small fees on the dollar volume and number of transactions processed across its network, plus cross-border fees.
originalCompanies.fact: Its 2008 IPO was the largest in U.S. history at the time, raising nearly $18 billion during the financial crisis.
originalCompanies.history: Shares dipped in 2020 as travel collapsed, then rose steadily as card spending and cross-border travel recovered.

originalCompanies.name: Walmart Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: The world’s largest retailer by revenue, operating thousands of supercenters, a warehouse club chain, and a growing e-commerce and advertising business.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells groceries and general merchandise at low margins and high volume, with membership fees and advertising adding higher-margin income.
originalCompanies.fact: Founded by Sam Walton in Arkansas; it is the largest private employer in the world.
originalCompanies.history: Shares were steady through the 2022 selloff as shoppers traded down, then rallied as e-commerce turned profitable; a 3-for-1 split took effect in 2024.

originalCompanies.name: The Coca-Cola Company
originalCompanies.blurb: Owns hundreds of soft drink, water, juice, and coffee brands sold in more than 200 countries, largely through independent bottling partners.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells concentrate and syrups to bottlers and earns brand licensing income; finished-goods sales add the remainder.
originalCompanies.fact: Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway has been a top shareholder since 1988; its secret formula is famously kept in a vault.
originalCompanies.history: A classic defensive stock: it held up well during the 2022 bear market and has raised its dividend for more than 60 consecutive years.

originalCompanies.name: The Walt Disney Company
originalCompanies.blurb: A global entertainment company spanning film studios, theme parks, cruise lines, cable sports networks, and streaming services.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Theme parks and consumer products generate the most profit, followed by sports networks, streaming subscriptions, and box office.
originalCompanies.fact: Founded by two brothers in 1923; a cartoon mouse became its most famous mascot.
originalCompanies.history: A streaming subscriber boom pushed shares to records in early 2021, then heavy streaming losses and a CEO change sent them down by more than half.

originalCompanies.name: NIKE, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: The world’s largest athletic footwear and apparel brand, selling through its own stores, apps, and wholesale partners.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells sneakers, apparel, and equipment, with footwear making up about two-thirds of revenue.
originalCompanies.fact: Started as Blue Ribbon Sports, importing Japanese running shoes; co-founder Phil Knight sold them from his car.
originalCompanies.history: Shares peaked in late 2021, then slid for years as a direct-to-consumer push backfired and competitors gained share.

originalCompanies.name: Intel Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: Designs and manufactures processors for PCs and servers and is building out a contract chip-manufacturing business.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells CPUs for laptops, desktops, and data centers; its foundry business currently loses money.
originalCompanies.fact: Co-founded by Gordon Moore, whose famous "law" predicted transistor counts would double roughly every two years.
originalCompanies.history: Lost manufacturing leadership and market share to rivals; shares fell by more than half in 2024 and the dividend was suspended.

originalCompanies.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Designs CPUs, graphics chips, and AI accelerators for PCs, game consoles, and data centers, outsourcing manufacturing.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Data-center processors and accelerators are its biggest segment, with PC chips, gaming console chips, and embedded products following.
originalCompanies.fact: Led by Lisa Su since 2014, it went from near bankruptcy to a major rival in server chips; it acquired Xilinx in 2022.
originalCompanies.history: Shares tripled from 2020 to late 2021 on server-chip share gains, fell in 2022, and rallied in 2023–24 on AI accelerator hopes.

originalCompanies.name: Costco Wholesale Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: Operates membership-only warehouse clubs selling a limited selection of products in bulk at very low markups.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Merchandise sales generate most revenue, but annual membership fees supply a large share of operating profit.
originalCompanies.fact: Its $1.50 hot dog and soda combo has kept the same price since 1985.
originalCompanies.history: A steady compounder that kept rising through the 2022 bear market thanks to loyal members and renewal rates above 90%.

originalCompanies.name: PepsiCo, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Sells snacks and beverages worldwide, owning many of the best-known chip, cereal, and soft drink brands.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Snack foods make up more than half of revenue, with beverages and packaged breakfast foods making up the rest.
originalCompanies.fact: Formed by the merger of a cola maker and Frito-Lay; its namesake drink was invented by a North Carolina pharmacist.
originalCompanies.history: Defensive strength helped in 2022, but volume declines and weight-loss-drug worries pushed shares lower in 2024–25.

originalCompanies.name: McDonald's Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: The largest fast-food chain in the world, with more than 40,000 restaurants, most owned by franchisees.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Collects rent and royalties from franchisees, which provides high-margin, stable income; company-operated stores add sales revenue.
originalCompanies.fact: Ray Kroc turned a single California burger stand into a global franchise; it is also one of the world’s largest real-estate owners.
originalCompanies.history: Resilient through the pandemic thanks to drive-thrus, it slipped in 2024 as cost-conscious customers pulled back.

originalCompanies.name: The Boeing Company
originalCompanies.blurb: Builds commercial jetliners, military aircraft, satellites, and defense systems and provides aircraft services.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells commercial airplanes to airlines and lessors, defense and space systems to governments, and maintenance services.
originalCompanies.fact: Founded by William Boeing in Seattle in 1916; one of only two major global makers of large passenger jets.
originalCompanies.history: Shares fell during the 2020 travel collapse, and quality problems including a 2024 door-plug blowout led to production caps and heavy losses.

originalCompanies.name: Exxon Mobil Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: One of the world’s largest publicly traded oil and gas companies, involved in exploration, production, refining, and chemicals.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Produces and sells crude oil and natural gas and refines them into fuels, lubricants, and petrochemicals.
originalCompanies.fact: Descended from John D. Rockefeller’s Standard Oil; it acquired Pioneer Natural Resources in 2024.
originalCompanies.history: Dropped out of the Dow in 2020 as oil prices collapsed, then more than doubled in 2022 when energy prices spiked, posting record profits.

originalCompanies.name: Johnson & Johnson
originalCompanies.blurb: A diversified healthcare company focused on prescription medicines and medical devices such as surgical and orthopedic products.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Innovative medicines (oncology, immunology) generate roughly two-thirds of revenue; medical technology supplies the rest.
originalCompanies.fact: Spun off its consumer health brands, including a famous baby shampoo and adhesive bandages, as Kenvue in 2023.
originalCompanies.history: A low-volatility stock that traded mostly sideways from 2021 to 2025 amid talc litigation and the consumer health spinoff.

originalCompanies.name: Pfizer Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: A large pharmaceutical company developing vaccines and medicines across oncology, immunology, and internal medicine.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells branded prescription drugs and vaccines to health systems and governments worldwide.
originalCompanies.fact: Partnered with BioNTech on the first COVID-19 vaccine authorized in the U.S., making it one of the best-selling drugs ever in 2022.
originalCompanies.history: Shares peaked in late 2021 on pandemic product sales, then lost more than half their value as that revenue faded.

originalCompanies.name: UnitedHealth Group Incorporated
originalCompanies.blurb: The largest U.S. health insurer, also running a huge healthcare services arm that includes pharmacy benefits, clinics, and data analytics.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Collects insurance premiums from employers, individuals, and government programs, plus fees from pharmacy and care-delivery services.
originalCompanies.fact: Its Optum unit is one of the largest employers of physicians in the United States.
originalCompanies.history: Long one of the steadiest large caps, shares plunged in 2025 after rising medical costs led it to suspend guidance and replace its CEO.

originalCompanies.name: Eli Lilly and Company
originalCompanies.blurb: A pharmaceutical company best known today for diabetes and obesity treatments, with additional drugs in oncology, immunology, and neuroscience.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells prescription medicines; GLP-1-based diabetes and weight-loss drugs are now its largest growth drivers.
originalCompanies.fact: Founded by a Civil War veteran and pharmacist; it was the first company to mass-produce insulin in the 1920s.
originalCompanies.history: Shares roughly quintupled from 2020 to 2024 as demand for its weight-loss drugs soared, making it the most valuable healthcare company in the world.

originalCompanies.name: Adobe Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Makes creative, document, and marketing software used by designers, photographers, video editors, and enterprises.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells subscriptions to its creative and document cloud suites and marketing analytics software.
originalCompanies.fact: Invented the PDF format; its photo-editing software name became a common verb.
originalCompanies.history: A pandemic darling that peaked in late 2021, it fell on a planned $20B Figma deal (later abandoned) and investor worries about generative AI competition.

originalCompanies.name: Salesforce, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: The leading provider of cloud-based customer relationship management software for sales, service, and marketing teams.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells subscriptions to its cloud software platforms, including analytics and workplace messaging products.
originalCompanies.fact: Founded by Marc Benioff, a former Oracle executive, pioneering the "no software" subscription model.
originalCompanies.history: Bought Slack in 2021 for about $27B, fell in 2022, then rallied in 2023 after activist investors pushed for higher margins.

originalCompanies.name: Oracle Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: Sells database software, enterprise applications, and cloud infrastructure, and has become a major provider of AI computing capacity.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Cloud services and software license support generate most revenue, followed by new licenses, hardware, and services.
originalCompanies.fact: Co-founded by Larry Ellison; it bought health-records company Cerner for about $28B in 2022.
originalCompanies.history: Long seen as a slow-growth software firm, shares more than doubled in 2024–25 as AI companies signed large cloud-capacity deals.

originalCompanies.name: PayPal Holdings, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Operates digital wallets and online payment processing for consumers and merchants, including a popular peer-to-peer payments app.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Earns transaction fees on payments processed for merchants, plus interest and fees from credit products.
originalCompanies.fact: Its early team, nicknamed the "mafia," went on to found or fund many major tech companies; it was owned by eBay before a 2015 spinoff.
originalCompanies.history: Soared during the pandemic e-commerce boom, then fell about 80% from its 2021 peak as growth slowed and competition intensified.

originalCompanies.name: Starbucks Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: The world’s largest coffeehouse chain, with tens of thousands of stores and a strong mobile ordering and loyalty program.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells beverages and food in company-operated stores, plus licensing and packaged coffee sold in grocery stores.
originalCompanies.fact: Named after a character in Moby-Dick; Howard Schultz turned it from a bean seller into a café chain.
originalCompanies.history: Hit records in 2021, then struggled with slowing traffic in the U.S. and China, leading to a CEO change in 2024.

originalCompanies.name: Uber Technologies, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Operates a global app connecting riders with drivers and customers with restaurants, grocery stores, and freight carriers.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Takes a cut of each ride, delivery, and freight booking processed through its platform, plus advertising.
originalCompanies.fact: Started as "UberCab" in San Francisco; it posted its first full year of operating profit in 2023.
originalCompanies.history: Shares fell below $25 in 2022, then more than tripled as the company reached sustained profitability and joined the S&P 500 in 2023.

originalCompanies.name: Caterpillar Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: The world’s largest maker of construction and mining equipment, diesel and gas engines, and industrial turbines.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells heavy machinery, engines, and replacement parts through a global dealer network, plus equipment financing.
originalCompanies.fact: Its iconic yellow machines are a bellwether for global construction and infrastructure spending.
originalCompanies.history: Infrastructure spending and strong pricing pushed shares to repeated records in 2023–24.

originalCompanies.name: The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: A leading global investment bank advising on mergers, underwriting securities, trading, and managing assets for institutions and wealthy clients.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Earns advisory and underwriting fees, trading revenue, and asset- and wealth-management fees.
originalCompanies.fact: Operated as a private partnership for 130 years before going public in 1999.
originalCompanies.history: Retreated from consumer banking in 2023 and rallied strongly in 2024 as trading and dealmaking rebounded.

originalCompanies.name: Bank of America Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: One of the largest U.S. banks, serving consumers, small businesses, corporations, and wealth-management clients.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Earns interest on loans and securities, plus fees from cards, investment banking, trading, and wealth management (Merrill).
originalCompanies.fact: Acquired Merrill Lynch in 2008 during the financial crisis; Berkshire Hathaway became its largest shareholder.
originalCompanies.history: Rising rates initially lifted profits in 2022, but unrealized losses on bond holdings weighed on shares during the 2023 banking scare.

originalCompanies.name: The Home Depot, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: The largest home improvement retailer in the U.S., serving do-it-yourself customers and professional contractors.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells building materials, tools, appliances, and garden supplies through about 2,300 big-box stores and online.
originalCompanies.fact: Its orange-apron stores were founded in Atlanta in 1978 by Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank.
originalCompanies.history: A pandemic home-renovation boom drove shares to records in 2021; higher mortgage rates and a slow housing market cooled growth afterward.

originalCompanies.name: The Procter & Gamble Company
originalCompanies.blurb: Makes everyday household and personal care products, owning many brands with more than $1 billion in annual sales each.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells branded consumer staples such as detergent, diapers, razors, and toothpaste through retailers worldwide.
originalCompanies.fact: Started by a candle maker and a soap maker; it essentially invented the modern brand-management system and the "soap opera."
originalCompanies.history: Price increases offset inflation in 2022–23, keeping the stock near record highs while the market fell.

originalCompanies.name: Ford Motor Company
originalCompanies.blurb: A century-old automaker selling trucks, SUVs, and commercial vans, investing heavily in electric vehicles.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells vehicles through dealers; trucks and commercial fleet vehicles generate most profit, while its EV unit loses money.
originalCompanies.fact: Pioneered the moving assembly line in 1913; the founder’s family still controls the company through special voting shares.
originalCompanies.history: EV excitement briefly tripled the share price in 2021–22 before supply-chain issues and EV losses pulled it back down.

originalCompanies.name: General Motors Company
originalCompanies.blurb: One of the largest U.S. automakers, selling trucks, SUVs, and electric vehicles under several brands, and running an autonomous-driving unit.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells vehicles through dealers, primarily high-margin pickups and SUVs in North America, plus auto financing.
originalCompanies.fact: Emerged from a government-backed bankruptcy in 2009 and returned to public markets with a record IPO in 2010.
originalCompanies.history: Shares more than doubled in 2021 on EV plans, then traded at low valuations amid strikes and EV slowdowns before buybacks lifted them in 2024.

originalCompanies.name: Moderna, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: A biotech company built around messenger RNA technology, developing vaccines and therapies for infectious diseases, cancer, and rare diseases.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells respiratory vaccines to governments and health systems; most other programs are still in clinical trials.
originalCompanies.fact: Its 2018 IPO was the largest biotech IPO ever at the time, years before it had any approved product.
originalCompanies.history: One of the best-performing stocks of 2020–21 at the height of the pandemic, it lost roughly 95% of its value as vaccine demand collapsed.

originalCompanies.name: Zoom Communications, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Provides video meetings, cloud phone systems, and team chat software used by businesses, schools, and consumers.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells monthly and annual subscriptions to its communications platform, mostly to businesses.
originalCompanies.fact: Its name became a verb during 2020 lockdowns, when daily meeting participants jumped from 10 million to 300 million.
originalCompanies.history: Shares rose about 400% in 2020 as the world went remote, then gave back nearly all of it as offices reopened.

originalCompanies.name: Broadcom Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Designs networking, wireless, and custom AI chips for data centers and smartphones, and sells infrastructure software after a string of acquisitions.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Semiconductor solutions (including custom AI accelerators) and enterprise infrastructure software each contribute large shares of revenue.
originalCompanies.fact: Built through serial acquisitions under CEO Hock Tan; it closed a roughly $69B purchase of VMware in 2023.
originalCompanies.history: Custom AI chip demand and the VMware deal helped shares climb more than sevenfold from 2020 to 2025; it completed a 10-for-1 split in 2024.

originalCompanies.name: Cisco Systems, Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: The largest maker of enterprise networking equipment such as routers and switches, with growing security and observability software lines.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells networking hardware plus recurring software subscriptions and support services to businesses and service providers.
originalCompanies.fact: Briefly the world’s most valuable company at the peak of the dot-com bubble in 2000.
originalCompanies.history: Traded in a range for years, then hit its highest level since 2000 in 2025 after acquiring Splunk and seeing AI networking demand.

originalCompanies.name: International Business Machines Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: A century-old technology company focused on hybrid cloud software, consulting, mainframe computers, and quantum computing research.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Software (including Red Hat) is the largest segment, followed by consulting services and infrastructure hardware.
originalCompanies.fact: Nicknamed "Big Blue"; its Deep Blue computer defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.
originalCompanies.history: Spun off its managed infrastructure unit as Kyndryl in 2021; software and AI momentum drove shares to record highs in 2024–25.

originalCompanies.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
originalCompanies.blurb: The world’s largest contract chipmaker, manufacturing the most advanced processors for many of the biggest chip design companies.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Charges chip designers to manufacture wafers on its leading-edge production lines; it does not sell chips under its own brand.
originalCompanies.fact: Founded by Morris Chang, it pioneered the "pure-play foundry" model of making chips only for other companies.
originalCompanies.history: Fell during the 2022 chip downturn, then surged on AI demand as it became the sole manufacturer of most leading AI accelerators.

originalCompanies.name: ASML Holding N.V.
originalCompanies.blurb: Builds the photolithography machines chipmakers use to print circuits onto silicon, including the only commercial extreme-ultraviolet systems.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells lithography systems that can cost over $150 million each, plus lucrative servicing and upgrades for its installed base.
originalCompanies.fact: Each of its flagship machines ships in dozens of crates and requires multiple cargo planes to deliver.
originalCompanies.history: A semiconductor supercycle lifted shares in 2021; export restrictions on China and a chip-spending slowdown triggered sharp drops in 2022 and late 2024.

originalCompanies.name: Shopify Inc.
originalCompanies.blurb: Provides software that lets merchants of all sizes build online stores, process payments, and manage inventory and point-of-sale.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Earns monthly subscription fees plus a share of payment processing and other merchant services volume.
originalCompanies.fact: Started when its founders were trying to sell snowboards online and found existing software lacking.
originalCompanies.history: Became Canada’s most valuable company in 2020, crashed about 80% in 2022, then recovered after selling its logistics arm.

originalCompanies.name: Novo Nordisk A/S
originalCompanies.blurb: A pharmaceutical company specializing in diabetes care that developed some of the first blockbuster weight-loss medications.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Sells insulin, GLP-1 diabetes treatments, and obesity drugs, primarily in the U.S. and Europe.
originalCompanies.fact: Became so large that its growth noticeably affected its home country’s GDP figures.
originalCompanies.history: Shares more than quadrupled to become Europe’s most valuable company in 2024, then fell sharply on disappointing trial data and competition.

originalCompanies.name: Sony Group Corporation
originalCompanies.blurb: A Japanese conglomerate spanning video game consoles, image sensors, music, movies, and consumer electronics.
originalCompanies.howItMakesMoney: Gaming is its largest segment, followed by music publishing and recording, image sensors, film, and electronics.
originalCompanies.fact: Created the Walkman portable cassette player in 1979; its image sensors are found in most premium smartphones.
originalCompanies.history: Its U.S. listing was among the first by a Japanese company; shares split 5-for-1 in 2024 and rose as gaming and anime businesses grew.
